title: 10 Animal Survival Superpowers, Explained by Science

intro.say: A frog that freezes solid and comes back to life. A bear that sleeps for months and never needs to pee. And a snail with teeth stronger than spider silk.
Animals have evolved some truly wild tricks to survive cold winters, hungry predators and tough jobs.
So here are ten animal survival superpowers, and the science that explains how they really work.

chapters.title: Why bears don't pee for months

scenes.say: Right now, bears are heading into their dens for the winter. A black bear can stay in there for up to seven months.
And during all that time, it doesn't eat, drink, pee or poop.
Its heart slows to about eight beats a minute, and it takes roughly one breath a minute. Its whole body runs on low power.
Normally, pee flushes out a waste called urea. Bears recycle it instead, and turn it back into protein for their muscles. Burning stored fat even makes water, so they don't need to drink.
A bear can lose up to a third of its weight by spring. But its muscles stay strong, because the waste is turned into muscle. The bear simply never needs to go.
Now meet an animal that takes winter even further. The wood frog freezes solid every year, and it isn't dead.
It lives so far north that its range crosses the Arctic Circle. When the frost comes, up to seventy percent of the water in its body turns to ice.
Its heart stops beating. Its brain goes quiet. It looks completely dead.
The trick is sugar. Its liver floods the body with it, like a natural antifreeze. The sugar keeps the ice outside its cells, so the cells don't burst.
It can survive minus sixteen degrees Celsius, frozen for months. In spring it thaws, heart and brain first, and is back to normal in about ten hours.

chapters.title: Do turtles really breathe through their butts?

scenes.say: You may have heard that turtles breathe through their butts in winter. It's a popular story online, but it isn't really true.
Painted turtles spend the winter at the bottom of frozen ponds, for months, with no way to reach the air for a single breath.
In 2004, scientists tested the butt idea and found no real gas exchange there. Instead, a little oxygen soaks in through their skin and the lining of their mouth.
When even that runs out, they can survive more than four months with no oxygen at all. Their heart slows to about one beat every few minutes.
Without oxygen, acid builds up in the body. So the turtle's shell releases minerals that soak it up. The real hero is the shell, not the butt.
Ducks stand on ice barefoot for hours. A duck's body is a warm forty one degrees Celsius, and the ice is zero. So why don't their feet freeze?
They use a trick engineers copy, called a heat exchanger. In the legs, warm arteries going down run right next to cold veins coming up.
The warm blood hands its heat to the cold blood before it reaches the feet. So the feet stay just above freezing, and the heat flows back into the body.
In one study, mallards at zero degrees lost only about five percent of their body heat through their feet. Penguins use the very same trick on the ice.
Still cold? A duck simply tucks one foot into its warm feathers and stands on the other. Not tough, just amazing plumbing.

chapters.title: Why geese fly in a V

scenes.say: In autumn, geese head south in a giant V. It's all about saving energy.
Each wingtip leaves a swirl of air that spins upward just behind it. The bird in back sits slightly to the side and surfs that rising air, a free ride.
In 2014, scientists tracked northern bald ibises flying in formation behind a small aircraft, and found the birds even time their flaps to match the bird ahead.
In a study of pelicans, birds at the back had lower heart rates than the leader. Flying in formation can save them up to eleven percent of their energy.
Leading is the hardest job, so tired leaders drop back and another bird takes over. No goose leads forever.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and there are more than fourteen hundred kinds of them. Almost all of them rest upside down.
The reason is takeoff. Their wings can't lift them from a standstill, and they can't run. So they hang up high, and to fly, they simply let go and drop.
Their body weight pulls on tendons that lock the claws shut. So gravity holds them up, and hanging costs almost no energy.
Their thigh bones are rotated a hundred and eighty degrees, so their knees bend the opposite way to ours.
Up on a cave ceiling, they're out of reach of owls, hawks and snakes. And because a bat must be awake to let go, it never drops off in its sleep.
A gorilla's chest beat looks like pure anger. But it's really a message, and it's one that can't lie.
Gorillas don't punch with fists. They beat with cupped hands, like a drum, and that deep pop can be heard more than a kilometer away.
Scientists recorded over five hundred chest beats from twenty five wild mountain gorillas in Rwanda. Bigger males made lower, deeper beats.
That's probably because big males have larger air sacs near their voice box. So rivals can hear how big a silverback is without even seeing him.
They can size each other up and skip a real fight. A chest beat is a size report made of sound.
Look closely at a beaver and you'll see orange teeth. That color comes from iron in their enamel, which makes the teeth extra tough.
Their front teeth never stop growing, so they have to keep chewing wood. A single beaver can cut down around two hundred trees a year.
All that wood builds dams that turn streams into deep ponds. Their lodges sit in that pond, with entrances hidden underwater. A beaver can hold its breath for about fifteen minutes.
In winter the deep water doesn't freeze solid, so the food they stored stays within reach, right below the ice.
The biggest beaver dam on Earth is about eight hundred and fifty meters long, in northern Canada. It's so big it was first spotted on satellite images.
A snail looks toothless. It isn't. Depending on the species, a snail can have two thousand to fifteen thousand tiny teeth.
They're not in a jaw like ours. They sit on a ribbon shaped tongue called a radula, covered in rows of teeth, like a tiny file.
The snail scrapes its food bit by bit, and the teeth wear down fast. So, a bit like a shark, it keeps growing new rows to replace them.
Its ocean cousin, the limpet, clings to rocks. In 2015, scientists found its teeth may be the strongest natural material ever tested, stronger than spider silk.
Each limpet tooth is under a millimeter long, and reinforced with an iron mineral called goethite. So that slow little snail is really a tongue full of teeth.

chapters.title: Why ladybugs bleed from their knees

scenes.say: That cute ladybug has a gross secret. When it's scared, it bleeds from its knees. Scientists call it reflex bleeding.
Yellow drops ooze out of its leg joints. That fluid is its blood, called hemolymph, and it's loaded with bitter, smelly chemicals.
A bird that grabs one gets a foul mouthful, and learns to leave ladybugs alone. That's what the bright red and black colors mean. They're a warning sign.
A seven spot ladybug can eat more than five thousand aphids in its lifetime. And radar has caught ladybugs flying over eleven hundred meters high.
Right now, in autumn, they gather by the thousands to sleep through the winter. So if you find yellow stains on your windowsill, that's not dirt. That's ladybug blood.

outro.say: So which superpower would you want? Freezing solid like the wood frog, sleeping for months like a bear, or iron teeth like a beaver? Tell us in the comments.
